transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-05-06
Start: 16:00 UTC
Duration: 62 minutes
Attendees: Samira Patel (Redwood AE), Liam Chen (Redwood SE), Derek Shaw (CTO - BlueHarbor), Maya Singh (Platform Lead), Jason Park (SRE), Elena Ruiz (Data Eng)

Auto Summary (auto-generated, may be rough):
Redwood ran a focused demo showing how the platform handles very long conversation history (50k+ tokens), high TPS bursts (~1k TPS sustained for short windows), and streaming backpressure/timeouts. The team discussed strategies: prefix/KV caching, truncation policies, graceful fallback to smaller model variants, circuit-breaker telemetry and telemetry thresholds. Customer requested a 48-72h POC with BlueHarbor prompts and asked for security docs and runbook.

Topics: long-context handling; KV cache eviction; streaming backpressure; per-token latency vs cost; dedicated capacity vs hosted; SSO/KMS questions; POC scope

Action items (captured above): see action_items metadata

Transcript body:
[00:00:05] Samira (Redwood AE): okay thanks everyone for joining, we're gonna run through a focused demo today on long session and surge behaviors, lee-m, sorry, liam will take the deep tech part, i'll do the kickoff and timeline.
[00:00:18] Derek (BlueHarbor): yep, appreciate it. Quick note, our main ask is we have chat sessions that can run up to, like, 40 to 80k tokens in history for some power users, and then bursts when our ingestion pipeline hits - we see 600 to 1k reqs per second for short windows. want to understand SLOs and cost.
[00:00:32] Samira: great context, that's the exact scenario we prepared for. quick qualification: are you planning hosted API first or a private VPC deployment?
[00:00:37] Maya: likely start hosted for eval, but we need the ability to go private for regulatory work later.
[00:00:44] Liam (Redwood SE): got it. i'll show host-mode first then how the same config maps to Dedicated/Private. note: some transcribed words below may be rough—our system sometimes spits Redwood as Redwoode in auto text—ignore that.
[00:00:58] Speaker 3 (Jason?): okay haha
[00:01:05] Liam: i'm going to pull up a replay. first principle: long history is handled two ways — prefix compression + KV cache reuse, and selective truncation/semantic pruning. we'll show both.
[00:01:20] [00:01:20] Liam: demo step 1: baseline run with full 60k token context against 1.2k token gen. watch latency tail.
[00:01:35] [00:01:35] (audio glitch)
[00:01:42] Derek: can you clarify, when you say KV cache reuse, that's per session or can it be shared across similar sessions?
[00:01:50] Liam: good q. KV cache is session-scoped by default for correctness, but you can configure shared prefix caches for templated flows. however we need to be careful with privacy — if you want session affinity and isolation, we keep it per-convo.
[00:02:08] Maya: and eviction? what causes it to drop? is it LRU?
[00:02:13] Liam: eviction is workload-aware; LRU-ish but we also weigh token recency and hit patterns. in high-tps surges we may shed older sessions to keep p50/p95 latency within SLO. that's where graceful fallbacks come in.
[00:02:28] Elena: when you say shed, do you mean you truncate history or slip to smaller model?
[00:02:34] Liam: both options exist. common pattern: first, truncate older message tails (semantic pruning), second, if memory pressure persists, route to a quantized model variant or smaller architecture — we call that a variant-fallback policy.
[00:02:46] [00:02:46] Samira: quick product note—console shows the fallback chain and the reason code (e.g., MEM_PRESSURE, QUEUE_DEPTH). you can set an automated policy to prefer cost-saving or latency-first actions.
[00:03:03] Jason: what's typical delta for token latency when you go from full to truncated?
[00:03:08] Liam: it depends on sequence length distribution; in our testbench a 60k->8k active context trimmed to recent 2-4k tokens can reduce per-token latency by 60-70% on CPU-bound paths; on GPU with optimized kernels it's more like 40-50% for long KV lookups. these are rough.
[00:03:28] [00:03:28] Derek: and cost math if we do variant fallback? smaller model is cheaper obviously, but what's the impact on quality?
[00:03:36] Liam: we include eval metrics side-by-side in Optimize — rouge/bleu-like and custom prompt set scoring. fallback loss is workload dependent; for many instruction flows smaller variants keep intent but may lose some nuance. we recommend canarying with A/B and automatic rollback if quality drops below threshold.
[00:03:55] [00:03:55] (brief overlap)
[00:04:02] Liam: demo time — running baseline. streaming window on the right shows chunked tokens and the stream buffer. notice at 00:04:20 we injected synthetic surplus traffic to emulate 1k TPS sustained for 30s.
[00:04:20] [00:04:20] (background typing)
[00:04:33] Samira: excuse me, if you look at console you'll see queue depth spike and a red box where the system bookmarked a fallback.
[00:04:41] [00:04:41] Speaker 5 (auto): (incoherent)
[00:04:52] Liam: ok the interesting bit — streaming backpressure: when buffer fills, we have three levers: backpressure signals to client (via stream status codes), internal chunk shedding (drop non-critical context), and request-level retry with jitter. we prefer to surface graceful partial results rather than hard timeouts.
[00:05:10] Maya: so you return partial streaming with a flag that indicates history was trimmed?
[00:05:15] Liam: exactly. there's a metadata header on responses like x-rw-fallback-reason: TRUNCATED_HISTORY or VARIANT_FALLBACK. that way your app knows to rehydrate or ask the model to summarize missing bits.
[00:05:28] Derek: that's helpful. what about client SDKs? do they automatically retry streaming chunks?
[00:05:33] Samira: our SDKs include built-in retry helpers and backoff presets. for high-throughput clients we recommend idempotent tokens and sticky routing if you want to preserve KV locality.
[00:05:45] [00:05:45] Jason: question on timeouts — we saw some earlier tests where long sessions had intermittent timeouts around 30s at p99. is that a gateway timeout or application-level?
[00:05:56] Liam: usually it's queue timeout. our gateway enforces a default request timeout of 60s for the hosted tier but internal worker queueing can cause per-chunk delays. we expose per-request tracing — you can see where time was spent: scheduling vs kernel execution vs prefix load.
[00:06:14] [00:06:14] (crosstalk)
[00:06:25] Liam: showing trace now — see red zones at scheduling during the surge. we can mitigate by increasing reserved concurrency pools (Dedicated), pre-warming model shards, or enabling per-customer burst lanes.
[00:06:38] Maya: is Dedicated the only way to guarantee no shedding?
[00:06:43] Liam: Dedicated gives you reserved GPU capacity so you're not competing with noisy neighbors. still, even on Dedicated you'll need truncation policies if a single session's history grows beyond device memory. we also support autoscale with hard caps.
[00:06:56] Derek: what about encryption and KMS—does KV cache get encrypted at rest?
[00:07:02] Samira: yes, for Private and Dedicated we support customer-managed keys (KMS/HSM). for hosted, keys are managed by us but we provide at-rest encryption and audit logs. we'll send the security FAQ.
[00:07:15] Derek: perfect.
[00:07:20] [00:07:20] Liam: jumping back to streaming backpressure — here's a failover demo: we intentionally saturate the stream buffer and step through the fallback chain: first serve partial result, then move to truncated context with variant fallback, finally queue-and-retry.
[00:07:36] [00:07:36] (audio artifact)
[00:07:45] Liam: note the streaming SDK will emit an event: onPartial(true) and include reason codes. apps can surface a "more context needed" CTA to the user.
[00:07:54] Maya: how do you recommend we instrument to detect quality regressions from fallbacks?
[00:08:00] Liam: use Optimize — attach prompt-level evals and baseline thresholds. also tag fallbacks in telemetry and run a daily sample of fallback responses through your eval harness. we include difference-in-quality alerts.
[00:08:15] Derek: ok curious — in your POC what should we provide to make it realistic?
[00:08:20] Samira: traffic traces (p50/p95/p99), sample convo threads with extremes, and the prompt/response expectations. we'll feed these into our benchmark harness.
[00:08:31] Elena: we have a couple of threads that include binary blobs and system messages, is Redwood able to strip or compress those automatically?
[00:08:39] Liam: we have preprocessors to strip non-text attachments and to compress repetitive tokens. you can also set semantic anchors so older segments compress to summaries preserved in the KV.
[00:08:52] [00:08:52] Speaker 6 (unlabeled): mm-hmm
[00:08:58] Samira: quick pause — does anyone have regulatory constraints that would block using hosted?
[00:09:04] Derek: for POC ok hosted, but eventual production for finance team needs VPC or private on-prem.
[00:09:10] Samira: that's fine; same APIs across Hosted/Dedicated/Private, so you can pilot hosted then migrate with config-only changes.
[00:09:20] [00:09:20] Liam: next i'd like to show telemetry: per-token cost breakouts, per-route latency, and an SLO guardrail UI that will trigger a canary rollback.
[00:09:31] [00:09:31] (screen share)
[00:09:38] Liam: here's an example failure scenario graph: notice when we triggered the 1k TPS burst, the p99 latency climbed then the SLO guard hit and we performed a transparent model switch for 12% of traffic (the blue band). app saw slightly degraded quality but stayed within latency SLO.
[00:09:56] Maya: can we force A/B to measure user impact?
[00:09:59] Liam: yes, canary rollout policies in Console let you route X% of traffic to fallback variant and measure eval metrics. you can configure automatic rollback if evaluation score delta > threshold.
[00:10:13] [00:10:13] Jason: question — can the console export raw traces to our Datadog?
[00:10:18] Samira: we support export to Datadog, Splunk, and cloud logging sinks. traces are OpenTelemetry-compatible with Redwood tags.
[00:10:27] [00:10:27] (short pause)
[00:10:33] Derek: switching gears — what about multi-tenant isolation if we want to run multiple product lines? we don't want one team to evict the other.
[00:10:42] Liam: we recommend per-tenant resource pools with quotas and separate KV namespaces. Dedicated can reserve pools per business unit. for hosted, enforce hard quotas and alerting.
[00:10:53] Maya: will that affect latency when tenants are idle and then spike?
[00:10:58] Liam: if reserved, you get predictable latency; if shared, spikes may cause shedding. autoscale can help but has ramp-up time.
[00:11:08] [00:11:08] (background noise)
[00:11:15] Samira: quick product note — Optimize will recommend batch sizes and quantization settings per route based on your traces. it's usually surprising how much throughput you can get with int8+kernel patches.
[00:11:28] Elena: any gotchas with int8 quantization and long context?
[00:11:33] Liam: quantization mainly impacts compute and sometimes output fidelity on precise numeric or token-level tasks. for long context, the main issue is memory layout; we do model-specific patching to avoid regression. during POC we'll include a quantized variant test.
[00:11:47] Derek: can you describe the worst-case behavior we should code for?
[00:11:52] Liam: worst-case: sudden surge + very large single session history causing memory saturation on shard -> request-level backpressure -> clients see partial responses or a 5xx while we shed. recommended app behavior: detect fallback headers, prompt user to retry or summarize, persist minimal context, and surface a "context truncated" UI.
[00:12:10] [00:12:10] (typing)
[00:12:19] Samira: i'm going to trigger a stress test now. we'll run three iterations: 1) baseline, 2) surge with preserved affinity, 3) surge without session affinity to show shedding patterns.
[00:12:33] [00:12:33] (test harness noise)
[00:12:48] [00:12:48] Liam: iteration one shows stable p95~180ms, p99~320ms. iteration two — with 1k TPS spike and sticky routing — p99 climbs but fewer session evictions. iteration three — no affinity — we see more KV reloads and higher overall cost due to more prefix rebuilds.
[00:13:05] Maya: cost numbers?
[00:13:08] Liam: in this synthetic, affinity reduced token egress cost by ~28% because we reused cached prefixes. exact numbers depend on your prompt redundancy.
[00:13:18] Derek: good to know. what about SDK observability hooks? can we surface cache hit/miss to our app?
[00:13:24] Samira: yes, SDK exposes metrics: cache_hit, cache_miss, fallback_reason, and stream_chunk_dropped. you can push these into your telemetry pipeline.
[00:13:36] [00:13:36] (reminder ping)
[00:13:44] Jason: we use strict SAML SSO and need role-based access — any concerns?
[00:13:49] Liam: Redwood supports SAML/SSO, RBAC, and audit logs; for private we can do SCIM provisioning. we'll attach the compliance pack.
[00:13:59] [00:13:59] (short pause)
[00:14:08] Derek: are there known failure modes with streaming and longcontext that we should test for specifically?
[00:14:14] Liam: yes — chunk reordering under network flakiness, partial-kv-eviction, and long-tail kernel stalls on very large attention windows. we have test suites and mitigations: chunk ACKs, replicated KV checkpointing, and kernel timeouts with fallback.
[00:14:33] Maya: can you show a kernel stall trace?
[00:14:36] Liam: yep — (screen) here's a 1.6s kernel stall during a 64k attention op on a particular model build; the system marked it as KERNEL_SLOW and retried on a warmed shard which completed at acceptable latency.
[00:14:50] [00:14:50] (laughter)
[00:14:57] Samira: circling back to POC scope — we'll need a couple of days of traffic to simulate weekend surges. can you do us a short doc describing the POC runbook?
[00:15:06] Liam: yes i'll prepare a POC runbook: objectives, traffic profile, metrics to capture, failure injectors, and success criteria.
[00:15:15] Derek: great. can we get pricing estimate for Dedicated vs hosted for the anticipated peak?
[00:15:20] Samira: i'll send a ballpark in the runbook and a formal quote after we size based on your traces.
[00:15:28] [00:15:28] (brief network artifact)
[00:15:35] Elena: small question: do you support token masking for PII redaction in flight?
[00:15:40] Liam: yes — we have pre-inference hooks and post-response sanitizers; for private you can run the sanitizer in customer network.
[00:15:49] [00:15:49] (crosstalk)
[00:15:55] Samira: alright last demo bit — failover to regional fallback. we'll simulate a region outage and show automated routing to secondary region and model variant.
[00:16:07] [00:16:07] (simulate failure)
[00:16:22] Liam: region failover introduced ~120ms extra RTT for requests but avoided service interruption. we logged a metric: region_fallback_count=1 and triggered an alert to ops.
[00:16:34] Derek: would that meet our finance team's SLA of <500ms tail?
[00:16:39] Liam: usually yes if you accept a small RTT hit; otherwise, Dedicated with multi-region replication is the path to preserve <500ms p99.
[00:16:48] [00:16:48] (note to self)
[00:16:55] Maya: i have one more question on billing — do you bill on tokens egress only or include KV cache loads?
[00:17:01] Samira: token billing is primary; there are also model runtime charges and storage for cached prefixes on Dedicated. we'll show detailed cost breakdown in the quote.
[00:17:12] [00:17:12] (silence)
[00:17:20] Liam: demo wrap-up — key recommendations: enable session affinity for high-reuse flows, set fallback policy 'latency-first' for UX-critical routes, run quantized variant A/B to save cost, and instrument fallback telemetry.
[00:17:33] Derek: sounds good. any gotchas for languages other than English?
[00:17:38] Liam: tokenization differences can change apparent context length. Optimize will surface per-language token inflation and suggest smaller batch sizes for some languages.
[00:17:49] [00:17:49] (screen share ends)
[00:17:55] Samira: ok practical next steps — we'll run a 48-72h POC, we'll need your traffic traces and sample conversation threads and we'll lock dates.
[00:18:03] Derek: we'll get those over by Monday.
[00:18:07] Maya: and security docs?
[00:18:10] Samira: yes, i'll send the security pack and the runbook together.
[00:18:15] [00:18:15] (small chatter)
[00:18:22] Liam: quick note on internal ops playbooks — if you hit streaming ttfb regressions, check kernel versions, check shard warming, and bump reserved concurrency temporarily; logs will show KERNEL_SLOW or MEM_PRESSURE.
[00:18:36] Derek: perfect, appreciate the level of detail.
[00:18:42] [00:18:42] (silence)
[00:18:50] Samira: ok we'll follow up with calendar invite for the POC kickoff and include Liam and Jason for the setup. any final quick questions?
[00:18:59] Jason: none from me.
[00:19:02] Maya: all good.
[00:19:05] Derek: thanks everyone.
[00:19:10] Samira: thanks all, talk soon.

(Transcript ends; note — timestamps after 00:19 represent the portion captured in detailed lines; the meeting continued with a short scheduling hangout and clarifications about doc attachments until 16:02 UTC.)
